articleTitle: Implementation of parallel control algorithms on a hypercube
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Parallel Processing: Industrial and Scientific Applications
abstract: Summary form only given. The author focuses on one particular aspect of parallel processing applied to control problems in the form of hypercube multiprocessors. The so-called distributed-memory hypercubes are exclusively considered in which the processors execute programs independently and communicate only by passing messages. The material presented begins with a review of the architecture and programming modes. Following this, algorithms and codes for solving a representative control systems problem, a Riccati equation are presented. A comparison of the performance of these against solutions run on other machines is given in the form of timing results. Finally, some on going work and future research areas are highlighted.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A transputer-based modular sensing system for robotic applications
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Parallel Processing: Industrial and Scientific Applications
abstract: In the majority of robotic systems currently available, a change in the type of sensors employed will require significant change to other parts of the system. The knock on effect caused by changes to sensors arises from the lack of independence between the different functions of current robotic systems. A transputer-based system is described where the sensors and the software that control them are separate from the processors that use the information they provide. This separation of data provider from data user enables the software that controls the sensors (and even the sensors themselves) to be upgraded with no corresponding changes to the data user software. Additional sensors can easily be added to the system while obsolete sensors can simply be removed. The nature of the task under consideration suggests that an extendible parallel architecture would be better suited to providing the processing requirements of such a system, than a traditional Von Neumann architecture. In general, one of the difficulties in using parallel architectures is that it is difficult to recognise inherent parallelism in problems. However, in this task the parallel operation of modules is self evident.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Fully connected transputer array for fault-tolerant real-time control
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Parallel Processing: Industrial and Scientific Applications
abstract: The widespread use of computers in the future will make people more dependent on them with the growing importance of reliability and safety. The observed trend of processing power to become cheaper will make more feasible the implementation of reliable computers based on hardware redundancy techniques. It is desirable for a computer system required to keep a plant under continuous control to tolerate faults with appear during its operation. The authors describe research in the properties of fully connected networks of 3 and 4 transputers with the aim of achieving enhanced reliability for real-time applications.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Parallel Processing: Industrial and Scientific Applications
abstract: A transputer array is used for visual texture analysis. The image is segmented and individual segments are sent to the transputer array to be analysed. The analysis technique is based on fractal texture measurements but modified to be suitable for non-fractal natural texture. Dynamic load balancing is used on the transputers in the array with software written in a modular fashion to facilitate changes in topology. Various topologies are used and their efficiencies are compared. Bottlenecks are identified and eliminated and 89% efficiency is achieved using an array of 16 transputers. Future avenues of investigation are discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Parallel Processing: Industrial and Scientific Applications
abstract: Agriculture and the production of food represent some of the most challenging environments for the application of computer systems. This paper reports the development of a system for grading vegetables and fruit. Because the unit value of even high quality vegetables is low, they must be inspected at high speeds to make a machine commercially worthwhile. In this work an image processing system was developed for grading potatoes at up to 2000 specimens per minute. The system is under the control of a Motorola 68000 processor which drives a specially designed data reduction unit operating directly on frames grabbed from the TV camera. The reduced data is routed to 4 further 68010 processors all of which are running concurrently. With the exception of the data reduction unit the system was designed around commercial processor cards communicating via a VME bus. This approach represents a practical solution to a real problem and the resulting system is now commercially available.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Parallel Processing: Industrial and Scientific Applications
abstract: The use of parallel processing techniques in obtaining real-time active damping of flexible beam structures is demonstrated using simulation. It is found that the overall computing can be split functionally into smaller sub-tasks which can be processed on tailor made architectures so that communication aspects are optimised. This flexibility in computer hardware configuration design is felt to be imperative if the control engineer is to successfully apply parallel techniques to a wide class of problems. The theoretical results presented need however to be implemented on a real system to assess their practical viability.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Design of parallel algorithms using discrete event simulation
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Parallel Processing: Industrial and Scientific Applications
abstract: Describes the transputer applications prototyping tool, Transim, and its graphical front end, Gecko. Transim is a simulation tool that reads an occam script with certain language extensions and produces information about the expected run-time performance. What makes Transim useful, however, is that the full code for the intended application is not required, Transim takes its input in the form of a control skeleton only, such as should be available early in the planning process. It is intended that the toolset is used early on in the software process as a kind of sketchpad, allowing ideas to be tested for performance more easily than fully coding and running them, yet more accurately than from back of the envelope calculations.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: High performance ATM network simulation using transputers
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Parallel Processing: Industrial and Scientific Applications
abstract: Considers a simulation application, using a network of transputers, which is designed to model ATM based telecommunication networks. It is primarily a distributed queueing network simulator which exploits independence between spatially separate events to process them concurrently. A routing process arrangement enables network topologies to be modelled without concern for the transputer interconnections. Additionally, despite the static allocation restrictions of OCCAM, different system topologies can be modelled without resorting to recompilation of the simulator program.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

abstract: This research is concerned with the development of a reliable scene analysis subsystem to continually update a geometrical world model in a robotic environment. The system uses parallel processing to implement a 3D model extraction algorithm.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Fault tolerant parallel processing architectures for safety-critical applications
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Parallel Processing: Industrial and Scientific Applications
abstract: With the advent of parallel processing redundancy, in the form of multiple microprocessors is automatically available. There is now much interest in trying to exploit this redundancy for fault tolerance while at the same time utilising the increased processing power. In such systems dynamic reconfiguration and graceful degradation can be employed presenting many interesting challenges to system developers. In the article the experiences of developing these systems using transputers for safety-critical real-time control systems is discussed. Although the work highlights aircraft applications many of the ideas proposed can be translated to other application areas.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: MasPar's MP-1 technology and its applications
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Parallel Processing: Industrial and Scientific Applications
abstract: Describes the MasPar MP-1 architecture and thereby demonstrates its potential for very high-performance; Describes MasPar's programming tools and environment; and illustrates the benefits obtained in porting applications packages on to MasPar computers. In describing these features the ease of programming and the realisation of very high performance for real applications is demonstrated.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Parallel algorithms applied to the stability analysis of 2D systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Parallel Processing: Industrial and Scientific Applications
abstract: Computation is, of course, a fundamental part of the design and implementation of control systems. It is used both off-line for functions such as simulation, analysis and synthesis of schemes and on-line for functions associated with implementations which use embedded processors. In the case of off-line functions, intensive research effort over the past two decades has provided efficient, reliable and portable tools for many of the common control systems design procedures. The success and maturity of this work has naturally led to a re-consideration of problems previously considered intractable from a computational standpoint. Such problems typically have models with state dimensions in the thousands and, for example, arise in complex distributed systems whose dynamics extend over wide frequency ranges or spatial domains. Further, considerable work has also been undertaken on extending the available techniques to other classes of systems. One such area is 2D linear systems which are the subject of this paper.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Application of transputers to the control of a batch distillation rig
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Parallel Processing: Industrial and Scientific Applications
abstract: The problem of controlling any complex process by its very nature requires a parallel solution for the control system. A transputer based architecture is compatible thus allowing a logical solution to the problem. Furthermore with the increased demands being placed on control systems a parallel process control solution is becoming more attractive. The authors demonstrate the parallel computer control of a batch distillation rig, using an array of transputers, and show the advantages and disadvantages of such a scheme against a realtime multitasking control system. The transputer network consists of a host T800 transputer, mounted in a PC, connected to a system of 11 other T800 transputers. The network transputers are able to communicate with the rig via special interface cards. The code on all the transputers is written in the Occam programming language.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Solving partial differential equations on a parallel supercomputer
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Parallel Processing: Industrial and Scientific Applications
abstract: In many engineering applications, the numerical solution of partial differential equations is required in the design and simulation of new products. Typically the speed and accuracy of such simulations have to be compromised by the user because of the limitations in computer power, resources and memory. As serial computers reach fundamental limits in performance, many engineers are turning to parallel computers to provide them with the computing power necessary for their design work. The iPSC/860 family of concurrent supercomputers gives the design engineer the computer power and memory for fast and accurate simulations. The iPSC/860 contains a number of processors or 'nodes', each with their own local memory. Calculations are carried out on data in a processor's local memory and data can be transferred between processors' local memory by message passing. There is no shared memory or shared resources to limit the scalability of the system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Parallel Processing: Industrial and Scientific Applications
abstract: Simulation software such as SIMBOL or TUTSIM allows systems to be described in block diagram form on screen. Each block represents a certain computation (often a transfer function) and when the software executes, it carries out the computations sequentially; there is therefore a proportional relationship between problem scale and execution time. However if the blocks are realised in hardware, nowadays digital hardware, this proportionality may be much reduced or may be removed, depending on the degree of parallelism. The authors describe the design of a completely parallel processing system-OMEGA- which is capable of implementing real time simulation on a very wide range of problems and which is much closer to the ethos of analogue computing than is current practice.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
